passages.title: Two promised births place mercy beside changed social standing
passages.summary: Luke says he has written an orderly account from eyewitness reports. An angel tells the old priest Zacharias that his wife will bear a son, John. Zacharias doubts and is made unable to speak. Gabriel tells Mary she will bear a son called the Son of the Most High. Mary visits Elizabeth, who blesses her. Mary sings that God has looked on her low position. John is born, and Zacharias speaks again. He praises God for raising up a savior.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from remembered or story settings. Emmaus, Nain, unnamed houses, and exact routes have no assigned marker.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies faithful responses and waiting through Mary, Elizabeth, and Zacharias. How does Mary’s song connect her own blessing with hungry and powerful people?

contextNote.title: Two promised births place mercy beside changed social standing
contextNote.text: Mary’s song begins with her own case. God has looked at the low position of his servant (verse 48). Verses 51–53 then widen to whole groups. God scatters the proud and brings rulers down. He lifts the lowly and fills the hungry. Verse 53 says the rich go away empty. Mary reads her own blessing as part of how God treats the poor.

passages.title: The joyful announcement does not remove the warning of pain
passages.summary: Caesar Augustus orders a registration, and Joseph and Mary travel to Bethlehem. Mary gives birth and lays her son in a feeding trough. Angels announce the birth to shepherds in the fields. The shepherds find the child and tell what they heard. In the temple old Simeon takes the child in his arms. He calls him a light for the nations and warns Mary of sorrow. The prophetess Anna gives thanks. At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple among the teachers.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Luke names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Why does Simeon place pain beside the promise of light?

contextNote.title: The joyful announcement does not remove the warning of pain
contextNote.text: Simeon first blesses God for salvation and light (verses 29–32). Then he turns to Mary with a warning. Verse 34 says the child will cause many to fall and rise. He will be a sign that people oppose. Verse 35 says a sword will pierce her own soul. The joy of the birth story is real. Luke sets the cost beside it from the start.

passages.title: Changed conduct answers the claim to inherited safety
passages.summary: In the fifteenth year of Tiberius, John preaches a baptism of repentance. He warns the crowds not to rely on descent from Abraham. The people ask what they should do. He tells them to share coats and food. Tax collectors must collect no more than is due. Soldiers must not extort money. John says one mightier than he is coming. Jesus is baptized, and Luke traces his family line back to Adam.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from remembered or story settings. Emmaus, Nain, unnamed houses, and exact routes have no assigned marker.

lds.text: The selected lesson reads changed conduct as evidence of repentance. How do John’s different answers address each group’s use of resources or power?

contextNote.title: Changed conduct answers the claim to inherited safety
contextNote.text: Three groups ask John the same question: what shall we do? His answers are specific. Verse 11 tells anyone with two coats to give one away. Verse 13 tells tax collectors to take only what is owed. Verse 14 tells soldiers not to use force for gain. Each answer fits that group’s money or power. Repentance is described as changed dealings with other people.

passages.title: The hometown claim meets examples of help beyond its boundaries
passages.summary: Jesus is tested by the devil in the desert for forty days. He returns to Galilee and teaches in the synagogues. In Nazareth he reads from Isaiah about good news for the poor. He says the Scripture is fulfilled that day. The people speak well of him at first. He reminds them that Elijah helped a foreign widow and Elisha a Syrian. They are furious and try to throw him off a cliff. He goes on to Capernaum and heals many.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Luke names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Why do the examples of Elijah and Elisha anger the hometown listeners?

contextNote.title: The hometown claim meets examples of help beyond its boundaries
contextNote.text: The people of Nazareth expect their own town to benefit (verse 23). Jesus answers with two stories from their Scriptures. Verse 26 recalls that Elijah was sent to a widow in Sidon. Verse 27 recalls that Elisha healed Naaman the Syrian. Both were outsiders, and Israel had many in need. The examples say God’s help is not owned by the home town. Verse 28 shows the room turning to rage.

passages.title: Following changes both work and the people welcomed at a meal
passages.summary: Jesus teaches from Simon’s boat and tells him to let down the nets. They catch so many fish that the nets begin to break. Simon, James, and John leave everything and follow him. He heals a man with a skin disease and a paralyzed man. He calls Levi, a tax collector, who leaves his booth. Levi gives a great feast with many tax collectors. Pharisees complain about the company. Jesus says he came to call sinners to repentance.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from remembered or story settings. Emmaus, Nain, unnamed houses, and exact routes have no assigned marker.

lds.text: How does the physician comparison explain the company at Levi’s meal?

contextNote.title: Following changes both work and the people welcomed at a meal
contextNote.text: Levi’s first act as a follower is to hold a feast (verse 29). His guests are other tax collectors. The Pharisees ask why Jesus eats with such people (verse 30). Verse 31 answers that the healthy do not need a doctor. Verse 32 states his purpose in the same terms. A doctor must be where the sick are. The meal is part of the call to repentance.

passages.title: The enemy command exceeds the exchange of favors
passages.summary: Jesus is challenged twice about the Sabbath. He spends a night in prayer and chooses twelve apostles. He teaches a great crowd on level ground. He blesses the poor and the hungry and warns the rich. He tells them to love their enemies and do good to those who hate them. They should lend and expect nothing back. They should not judge, and they should forgive. The one who hears and acts builds on rock.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from remembered or story settings. Emmaus, Nain, unnamed houses, and exact routes have no assigned marker.

lds.text: Why does love for enemies go beyond exchanging equal favors?

contextNote.title: The enemy command exceeds the exchange of favors
contextNote.text: Verses 32–34 examine ordinary fairness. People love those who love them and lend to those who repay. Jesus says even sinners do that. Verse 35 asks for more: love enemies and lend with no return. The reason given is God’s own conduct. He is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. Verse 36 sums it up as mercy like the Father’s.

passages.title: A host's judgment fails to see the care before him
passages.summary: Jesus heals a Roman officer’s servant from a distance. At Nain he raises a widow’s only son. John the Baptist sends to ask whether Jesus is the one to come. A Pharisee named Simon invites Jesus to dinner. A woman known as a sinner weeps over his feet and anoints them. Simon thinks a prophet would know what she is. Jesus tells of two debtors forgiven different amounts. He tells the woman that her sins are forgiven.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers distinguish events from remembered or story settings. Emmaus, Nain, unnamed houses, and exact routes have no assigned marker.

lds.text: What does Simon fail to see before Jesus compares their acts of welcome?

contextNote.title: A host's judgment fails to see the care before him
contextNote.text: Simon looks at the woman and sees only her past (verse 39). In verse 44 Jesus asks him, “Do you see this woman?” Then he compares host and guest. Simon gave no water, no kiss, and no oil. She gave tears, kisses, and perfume. The host skipped the ordinary courtesies, and she went far past them. Simon judged her and missed the care in front of him.

passages.title: Hearing becomes action through support, witness, and restored life
passages.summary: Jesus travels with the twelve and with women who support them from their own means. He tells of a farmer sowing seed on four soils. His mother and brothers cannot reach him through the crowd. He says his family are those who hear God’s word and do it. He calms a storm on the lake. He frees a man from many demons. A woman with long bleeding is healed. He raises the daughter of Jairus.

lds.text: How does the family saying join hearing with doing?

contextNote.title: Hearing becomes action through support, witness, and restored life
contextNote.text: The farmer’s story ends with seed in good soil (verse 15). Such people hear the word, hold it, and bear fruit. Verse 21 says the same thing about family. His mother and brothers are those who hear and do. The chapter begins with an example. Verses 2–3 name women who pay for the group’s needs. Hearing has become action in their case.

passages.title: The Jerusalem journey rejects the disciples' desired retaliation
passages.summary: Jesus sends the twelve to preach and heal, and he feeds five thousand. Peter says he is the Christ of God. Jesus says he must suffer and that followers must take up their cross daily. He is changed in appearance on a mountain. The disciples argue over who is greatest. Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem. A Samaritan village refuses him. James and John want to call down fire, and he rebukes them.

lds.text: Why does Jesus reject the disciples’ proposed fire?

contextNote.title: The Jerusalem journey rejects the disciples' desired retaliation
contextNote.text: Verse 51 begins the long journey to Jerusalem. The first village on the way refuses to receive him (verse 53). James and John offer to call fire from heaven (verse 54). Elijah once did so in 2 Kings 1:10–12. Verse 55 says Jesus turned and rebuked them. They simply go on to another village (verse 56). He will not answer rejection with destruction.

passages.title: The neighbor question changes from a boundary to an action
passages.summary: Jesus sends seventy others ahead of him in pairs. They return with joy at what they have done. A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. He agrees that the law says to love God and neighbor. He then asks who his neighbor is. Jesus tells of a man beaten by robbers and left half dead. A priest and a Levite pass by, and a Samaritan cares for him. Jesus then visits Martha and Mary.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Luke names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects neighbor love with the Samaritan’s practical care. How does the final neighbor question change the lawyer’s original question?

contextNote.title: The neighbor question changes from a boundary to an action
contextNote.text: The lawyer asks who his neighbor is (verse 29). He wants to know where his duty stops. Jesus tells the story and then changes the question. Verse 36 asks which of the three became a neighbor to the wounded man. The word now describes what a person does. The lawyer cannot bring himself to say “Samaritan.” He answers, “He who showed mercy” (verse 37).

passages.title: Clean surfaces cannot replace justice and help with burdens
passages.summary: Jesus teaches his disciples a prayer and tells them to keep asking. Some say he drives out demons by their ruler. He says a divided kingdom falls. He warns that this generation seeks a sign. A Pharisee invites him to a meal and is surprised he does not wash. Jesus says they clean the outside of the cup. They tithe herbs and pass over justice and God’s love. He says the lawyers load people with burdens.

lds.text: What connects clean surfaces with neglected justice in the meal dispute?

contextNote.title: Clean surfaces cannot replace justice and help with burdens
contextNote.text: The dispute begins over washing before a meal (verse 38). Verse 39 says the outside is clean and the inside is full of greed. Verse 42 gives a second example. These men tithe every garden herb. Jesus does not object to that. He says they have passed over justice and the love of God. Verse 46 adds that they load others and will not lift a finger.

passages.title: Waiting tests the way entrusted power treats others
passages.summary: Jesus warns a great crowd against hypocrisy and fear of people. A man asks him to settle an inheritance. He tells of a rich man who built bigger barns and died that night. He tells his disciples not to worry about food or clothes. They should sell what they have and give to the poor. They should be like servants waiting for their master. Much is required of the one given much. He says he has come to bring division.

lds.text: How does the returning master’s service change expectations about power?

contextNote.title: Waiting tests the way entrusted power treats others
contextNote.text: Verse 37 describes servants who are awake when their master returns. What follows is unexpected. The master dresses for service and has them sit down. He then waits on them himself. Masters did not do this (see 17:7–8). Verses 42–46 give the other side for those set over the household. A manager who beats the servants during the wait is punished.

passages.title: Repentance does not require blaming victims for their suffering
passages.summary: People tell Jesus about Galileans whom Pilate killed. He asks whether they were worse sinners than others. He says no, and that everyone must repent. He tells of a fig tree given one more year. On a Sabbath he heals a woman bent over for eighteen years. The synagogue ruler objects. Jesus says she is a daughter of Abraham and should be set free. He weeps over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets.

lds.text: Why does Jesus reject greater guilt as the explanation for the victims’ deaths?

contextNote.title: Repentance does not require blaming victims for their suffering
contextNote.text: Verses 1–5 mention two disasters. Jesus rejects the idea that the victims were worse than others. He calls everyone to repent and blames none of the dead. The healing in verses 10–16 follows the same line. The woman’s long illness is not treated as her fault. Verse 16 calls her “a daughter of Abraham.” She has every right to be freed, and the Sabbath is the right day.

passages.title: The meal's invitations challenge the expectation of repayment
passages.summary: Jesus eats at a leading Pharisee’s house on the Sabbath and heals a man there. He sees guests choosing the best seats. He tells them to take the lowest place. He tells his host to invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind. He tells of a great banquet whose invited guests make excuses. The host fills his house from the streets and lanes. Jesus tells the crowds to count the cost of following him. Salt that loses its taste is thrown out.

lds.text: How does inviting people unable to repay challenge the host’s expectations?

contextNote.title: The meal's invitations challenge the expectation of repayment
contextNote.text: Verse 12 names the usual guests: friends, brothers, relatives, and rich neighbors. They will invite the host in return. Verse 13 names a different list. The poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind cannot repay. Verse 14 says that is the point. A meal given for return is a trade. Jesus asks for a table where no payment is possible.

passages.title: The celebration leaves the older brother with a decision
passages.summary: Tax collectors and sinners gather to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees grumble. He tells of a shepherd who finds one lost sheep. He tells of a woman who finds one lost coin. He tells of a man with two sons. The younger wastes his share and comes home hungry. The father runs to him and holds a feast. The older son is angry and will not go in. The father comes out and pleads with him.

lds.text: Why does the story end with the father’s appeal rather than the older son’s decision?

contextNote.title: The celebration leaves the older brother with a decision
contextNote.text: The story has two sons, and both end up outside the house. The younger returns and is welcomed. The older stands in the yard and refuses to enter (verse 28). The father comes out to him as well. Verse 32 gives the father’s last appeal: “this, your brother.” The story stops there. Jesus’s hearers in verse 2 are left to decide whether to go in.

passages.title: Possessions and listening connect the two difficult stories
passages.summary: Jesus tells of a dishonest manager who reduces debts to win friends. He says no servant can serve two masters. The Pharisees, who love money, scoff. He tells of a rich man who feasted every day. A poor man named Lazarus lay at his gate covered with sores. Both die, and Lazarus is comforted at Abraham’s side. The rich man asks that Lazarus warn his brothers. Abraham says they have Moses and the prophets.

lds.text: Why does Abraham point the brothers toward words they already have?

contextNote.title: Possessions and listening connect the two difficult stories
contextNote.text: Lazarus lay at the rich man’s gate every day (verse 20). The rich man knew his name (verse 24). In torment he asks for a messenger from the dead for his brothers. Verse 31 refuses. They already have Moses and the prophets. Those writings say plainly how to treat the poor. A miracle would not persuade people who ignore them.

passages.title: The foreigner's return makes gratitude visible
passages.summary: Jesus warns against causing others to stumble and tells his disciples to forgive. A servant does not expect thanks for doing his duty. Between Samaria and Galilee ten men with a skin disease cry out for mercy. Jesus tells them to show themselves to the priests. They are healed as they go. One returns, praises God, and thanks Jesus, and he is a Samaritan. The Pharisees ask when God’s Kingdom will come. Jesus says it will come like lightning.

lds.text: Why does Jesus identify the returning man as a foreigner?

contextNote.title: The foreigner's return makes gratitude visible
contextNote.text: All ten men are healed on the road (verse 14). Nine keep walking. One turns back and praises God in a loud voice. Verse 16 adds a detail: “He was a Samaritan.” Verse 18 calls him “this foreigner.” The outsider is the one who gives thanks. Verse 19 tells him that his faith has made him well.

passages.title: The tax collector's prayer contrasts with a list of achievements
passages.summary: Jesus tells of a widow who keeps asking an unjust judge for justice. He tells of two men who pray in the temple. A Pharisee thanks God that he is not like other people. A tax collector asks only for mercy. People bring infants, and Jesus welcomes them. A rich ruler asks about eternal life and leaves sad. Jesus foretells his death again. Near Jericho he gives sight to a blind beggar.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches trust in God’s mercy rather than condemning others through self-praise. How does the tax collector’s prayer differ from the Pharisee’s comparisons?

contextNote.title: The tax collector's prayer contrasts with a list of achievements
contextNote.text: The Pharisee’s prayer in verses 11–12 is a list. He names what he avoids and what he gives. He compares himself with the man behind him. ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study. Luke 10:30 sets a parable on the way down from Jerusalem to Jericho.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

regions.name: Herod’s kingdom · approximate
regions.summary: Herod the Great ruled as king under Rome from 37 to 4 BCE. His kingdom held Judea, Samaria, Galilee, and lands east of the Jordan.
regions.detail: Luke 1:5 sets the story of Zacharias in the days of Herod, Judea’s king.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the regions the article lists.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Luke 2:2 dates a census by Quirinius, governor of Syria.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Pontius Pilate governs Judea in the Gospels (Luke 3:1). He tries Jesus in Jerusalem.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

regions.name: Galilee · under Herod Antipas
regions.summary: Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea until 39 CE.
regions.detail: Jesus grows up and teaches in Galilee under Antipas. Antipas kills John the Baptist (Mark 6).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to Galilee.

regions.name: Perea · under Herod Antipas
regions.summary: Perea lay east of the Jordan, across from Judea and Samaria. Herod Antipas ruled it with Galilee.
regions.detail: Matthew 19:1 and Mark 10:1 take Jesus beyond the Jordan. He is on his way to Jerusalem.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The Gospels do not use the name Perea.

regions.name: Philip’s lands · approximate
regions.summary: Philip, another son of Herod, ruled lands northeast of the Jordan until 34 CE.
regions.detail: Luke 3:1 names Philip as tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis. A tetrarch ruled one part of a divided kingdom.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Syria took these lands after Philip died.

regions.name: Decapolis · approximate
regions.summary: The Decapolis was a group of ten Greek-style cities, most east of the Jordan. Each ran itself under Rome.
regions.detail: Crowds from the Decapolis follow Jesus (Matthew 4:25). The healed man of Mark 5 tells his story there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape covers the southern cities only. Some scholars doubt the cities formed one league.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Luke 2:2 dates a census by Quirinius, governor of Syria. Jesus visits the coast near Tyre and Sidon in Mark 7:24.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

guides.title: Luke: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: The hometown claim meets examples of help beyond its boundaries
steps.text: The people of Nazareth expect their own town to benefit (verse 23). Jesus answers with two stories from their Scriptures. Verse 26 recalls that Elijah was sent to a widow in Sidon. Verse 27 recalls that Elisha healed Naaman the Syrian. Both were outsiders, and Israel had many in need. The examples say God’s help is not owned by the home town. Verse 28 shows the room turning to rage.

steps.title: The neighbor question changes from a boundary to an action
steps.text: The lawyer asks who his neighbor is (verse 29). He wants to know where his duty stops. Jesus tells the story and then changes the question. Verse 36 asks which of the three became a neighbor to the wounded man. The word now describes what a person does. The lawyer cannot bring himself to say “Samaritan.” He answers, “He who showed mercy” (verse 37).

steps.title: The celebration leaves the older brother with a decision
steps.text: The story has two sons, and both end up outside the house. The younger returns and is welcomed. The older stands in the yard and refuses to enter (verse 28). The father comes out to him as well. Verse 32 gives the father’s last appeal: “this, your brother.” The story stops there. Jesus’s hearers in verse 2 are left to decide whether to go in.

steps.title: Remembered words and shared bread change disappointed recognition
steps.text: The two travelers say, “we were hoping” (verse 21). Their hope is in the past tense. The stranger walks with them and explains Moses and the prophets (verse 27). They know him only when he breaks the bread (verses 30–31). Verse 32 looks back on the road. Their hearts had been burning while he opened the Scriptures. Explained words and a shared meal together bring recognition.

chapterMaps.narrative: Luke says he has written an orderly account from eyewitness reports. An angel tells the old priest Zacharias that his wife will bear a son, John. Zacharias doubts and is made unable to speak. Gabriel tells Mary she will bear a son called the Son of the Most High. Mary visits Elizabeth, who blesses her. Mary sings that God has looked on her low position. John is born, and Zacharias speaks again. He praises God for raising up a savior.

He calls him a light for the nations and warns Mary of sorrow. The prophetess Anna gives thanks. At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple among the teachers.

Jesus is baptized, and Luke traces his family line back to Adam.

They are furious and try to throw him off a cliff. He goes on to Capernaum and heals many.
